note:
605 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar defeated a coalition of Assyria and Egypt at Carche­mish and initiated Babylon’s rise to international power. After the battle of Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar advanced against Jehoiakim (2 Kin. 24:1, 2; 2 Chr. 36:5–7) and took some Judeans captive, including Daniel. This was the first of three invasions of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar. The second was in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:10–14), and the third in 586 B.C. (2 Kin. 25:1–24). In the book of Jeremiah, Nebuchadnezzar’s attack is dated to Jehoiakim’s fourth year instead of the third (Jer. 25:1; 46:2). The difference occurs because in the Babylonian chronology, which Daniel apparently used, the king’s reign was officially counted from the first day of the succeeding new year, rather than from the actual date of his accession to the throne.

**Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.** Neb­uchadnezzar led the Babylonians to victory at Carchemish as crown prince and commander of the army. Shortly after this victory, he assumed the Babylonian throne when his father Nabopo­lassar died (626–605 B.C.). Nebuchadnezzar’s reign (605–562 B.C.) is the historical context for much of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

verse_quote: the Lord gave ... into his hand.
note:
Israel’s defeat by the Babylonians is not to be explained simply by analysis of military and political factors. God is at work in the affairs of the nations, and the message to Daniel’s original audience is that He has used the Babylonians to judge His own people for their transgressions (2 Kin. 17:15, 18–20; 21:12–15; 24:3, 4). Under the terms of the covenant made at Mount Sinai, the Lord threatened to exile His people if they were unfaithful (Lev. 26:33, 39). The length of their tenure in the land in spite of their unfaithfulness is a sign of the Lord’s mercy. Their unfaithfulness culminated in the destruction of Jerusalem and exile of the majority of the remaining population by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C.

**the vessels of the house of God.** These same temple vessels are brought out by Belshazzar for his feast in Dan. 5 and will be returned to Judah with the exiles in the time of Cyrus (Ezra 1:7).

**the treasury of his god.** Marduk (or Bel) is the chief god of the Babylonian pantheon (cf. Jer. 50:2).

Like the temple vessels and sacrifices, they have to be perfect to appear in the presence of the king. The exiling of these royal and noble offspring fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy to King Hezekiah in 2 Kin. 20:17, 18.

**literature and language of the Chaldeans.** Babylonian literature was written in Akkadian, using wedge-shaped characters impressed with a stylus on soft clay tablets that were later fired to make them permanent. Thousands of these tablets have been discovered by archaeologists. The Babylonians worshiped many gods, and their culture was filled with magic, sorcery, and astrology. The common commercial language of Babylon was Aramaic, which was used especially in the court of the king during the time of Daniel (see 2:4 and note).

verse_quote: the food that the king ate.
note: KingJehoiachin later receives such a provision under the rule of the Babylonian king Evil-merodach (2 Kin. 25:27–30). These provisions are designed to create a culture of dependence on the king.

These Hebrew names contain the word “God” (_el_) or a shortened form of God’s covenant name, “Yahweh” (Ps. 50:1 note). Daniel means “my judge is God”; Hananiah, “Yahweh is gracious”; Mishael, “Who is what God is?”; and Azariah, “Yahweh has helped.”

Suggestions for the meanings of these names include: Belteshazzar, “May Bel protect his life” (Bel is another name for Marduk, the chief Babylonian god; cf. 4:8); Shadrach, “the command of Aku,” (the Sumerian moon god); Meshach, “Who is what Aku is?”; and Abednego, “servant of Nebo” (a Babylonian god). These name changes are a further step in Babylon’s attempt to reshape their religious and cultural identity.

The reason for Daniel’s conclusion that he and his friends will be defiled by the king’s food is not given. Perhaps it involves violation of the dietary laws of Moses (Lev. 11; 17). Yet it does not appear that they permanently abstain from Babylonian food, as would be required if the issue were obedience to the kosher laws. More likely, this is a concrete way of affirming their dependence upon the Lord by vowing to eat only foods that grow naturally and to drink only water rather than to consume the rich food and wine provided by the king.
This is a specific answer to Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple in 1 Kin. 8:50.

That is, they are fatter—an unexpected result of a low-calorie lifestyle. The obedience of Daniel and his friends to God and their refusal to compromise their faith in a heathen environment are rewarded with God’s blessing (cf. Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4).

God’s blessing is not limited to physical well-being, but also includes outstanding intellectual development during their three years of Babylonian education. He thus enables them to be a blessing to their pagan neighbors and to build up the city where they have found themselves (cf. Jer. 29:5–7) while remaining true to their beliefs.

**visions and dreams.** With a view to what follows in the book (chs. 2; 4; 5), Daniel is distinguished from his companions in his ability to interpret dreams and visions, much as Joseph was in the court of Pharaoh (Gen. 40:8; 41:16).

verse_quote: At the end of the time.
note: That is, after the three years mentioned in v. 5.

The term translated “magicians” is also used in Gen. 41:8, 24, and Ex. 7:11. The word translated “enchanters” occurs only here and in 2:2 and can be rendered “conjurer” or “soothsayer.” Whatever means these royal advisers use to gain knowledge, Daniel and his friends are able to demonstrate superior insight on the matters they were questioned about.

verse_quote: until the first year of King Cyrus.
note: Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 B.C., sixty-six years after Daniel had been taken captive to Babylon. Daniel lived through the entire period of the Babylonian captivity. Cyrus issued a decree in the first year of his reign permitting the Jews to return to their land, and to take with them the vessels from the temple that had been seized by Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 1:7–11). The statement does not mean that Daniel died in the first year of Cyrus (10:1), but rather that the Lord was faithful to protect Daniel all the way through the exile. Kingdoms might rise and fall, but the Lord preserves His own.

Since the Babylonian system counts Nebuchadnezzar’s reign officially from the first day of the year after his actual accession, his “second year” could mean the end of Daniel’s three years of training (1:5). Otherwise the events took place during his training.

**his sleep left him.** It was widely believed in the ancient Near East that the gods spoke to human beings in dreams. The dreams of a king had particular significance for the fate of the whole people.

See note on 1:20.

**sorcerers ... Chaldeans.** “Sorcerers” practice divination or witchcraft (Ex. 22:18; Deut. 18:10; Is. 47:9, 12; Jer. 27:9). Here, “Chaldeans” probably means a class of soothsayers and astrologers, rather than the name of an ethnic group (as in 1:4; 3:8; 5:30; 9:1). These are part of Nebuchadnezzar’s specialist staff of dream interpreters.

From here until the end of ch. 7, the text is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. Ezra 4:8–6:18; 7:12–26 are also written in Aramaic. There has been much speculation about why these verses are in Aramaic, but no generally accepted conclusion has been reached.

verse_quote: make known to me the dream.
note: Normally, the king would tell his advisors the dream so that they could suggest an interpretation. Here, Nebuchadnezzar formulates a test to see whether the advisors to the court have the access to hidden knowledge that they claim. If they cannot tell him the dream, then he will have no confidence in their interpretation (cf. v. 9) and will execute them.

The wise men confess that they cannot do what the king asks. Only the gods have such power, but the gods, they protest, do not reveal such things to anyone (cf. Ex. 8:18, 19). They are diviners, not prophets: they discern patterns in events but do not claim access to the minds of the gods. Indeed, in their theology, such knowledge is impossible since the gods do not make their dwelling among men. Israel’s God is unique in this respect (see Is. 57:13).

verse_quote: all the wise men of Babylon.
note: Nebuchadnezzar’s furious response expands the group subject to punishment to include the whole class of wise men, including Daniel and his friends. With remarkable confidence, Daniel asks for an appointment to see the king, even though he has yet to receive revelation from God.

verse_quote: seek mercy from the God of heaven.
note: Daniel also realizes that human wisdom is insufficient to meet the king’s demand (v. 11 note). Only divine revelation can provide the answer. Fortunately, unlike the gods of the Babylonians, Daniel’s God is able and willing to reveal what will happen in the future (Is. 44:8; 45:21; Amos 3:7)., 19
See theological note “The Will of God.”

verse_quote: he removes kings and sets up kings.
note: Daniel alludes to the content of the dream.

verse_quote: he reveals deep and hidden things.
note: Job 28 is a carefully drawn picture of wisdom as “hidden from the eyes of all” (Job 28:21) and inaccessible without God.

verse_quote: Do not destroy the wise men.
note: Daniel urges the king to be merciful to the wise men even though their inability to know the dream has been exposed.
Arioch is eager to claim credit for finding someone who can interpret the king’s dream.

verse_quote: a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.
note:
Just as Joseph did in Egypt (Gen. 40:8; 41:16), Daniel attributes his knowledge of the dream to God. Daniel’s God has revealed to this young man what astrology, magic, and the occult cannot discover.

**in the latter days.** This expression seems to range in meaning from the “end time” or _eschaton_(Gk.; cf. Ezek. 38:16) to simply the future in general (Gen. 49:1; Deut. 4:30; 31:29). Here it covers the entire sweep of world history from Nebuchadnezzar onward.
There is a progressive decrease in the value of the materials in the image from the head to the feet., 33

verse_quote: its feet of iron and clay.
note: Some interpreters view the mixture of iron and clay in the feet of the image as representing a second phase of the fourth kingdom different from the legs of solid iron (cf. vv. 41–43).

The four kingdoms have been widely understood since the Jewish historian Josephus (writing in the first century A.D.) to be the empires of Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome. Others understand them to be Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, a sequence in agreement with the liberal critical view that the book was written during the period of Greek ascendancy in the Middle East. Darius’s appeal to the single “law of the Medes and Persians” (6:12; cf. 5:28) agrees with the first order of empires.

The only certain identification between the portions of the image and specific world empires is Nebuchadnezzar (Babylon) as the head of gold. It is plausible that four represents completeness here: rather than seeking to describe particular kingdoms, the sequence describes the consistent downward trend in world history, not toward greater glory and unity but toward greater dishonor and chaos until the kingdom of God arrives on earth and fills it with its glory. The rock that crushes all of the kingdoms of this world is Christ (Luke 20:18). He is the mystery of the ages, the One in whom God will unite all things in His glorious kingdom (Eph. 1:9, 10).

verse_quote: they will mix ... but ... not hold together.
note: The elements of the fourth kingdom cannot preserve their union. One possible interpretation of the image is that the iron represents the culture and laws of imperial Rome, while the clay represents the divergent political and social traditions of its many parts. The fourth kingdom, though strong, is as temporary as those that precede it and lacks the glory of the earlier kingdoms.

The most natural interpretation is that the kings are the rulers of the four powers making up the image just described. The other possibility is that they are a sequence of several rulers of the fourth kingdom only.

**a kingdom that shall never be destroyed.** The eternal kingdom is the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ (Is. 9:7; Luke 1:33; Heb. 1:8; Rev. 11:15). This kingdom was inaugurated and preached at the first coming of Christ (Matt. 12:28; 24:14; Mark 1:15) but does not come in its fullness until His second coming. See theological note “The Kingdom of God” on p. 1823.

verse_quote: King Nebuchadnezzar fell ... paid homage to Daniel.
note: In a reversal of roles, Daniel is exalted to a position of honor by the Lord’s intervention on his behalf, from which he and his friends will be able to promote the peace and welfare of the city of Babylon where God has placed them (Jer. 29:5–7). For the king’s reaction, cf. Acts 14:11; Rev. 22:8.

Nebuchadnezzar’s statement does not necessarily mean that he recognizes Israel’s covenant Lord, Yahweh, as the only God. His exclamation is that Yahweh is superior to other gods.

**Lord of kings.** Nebuchadnezzar confesses that the God of Israel is supreme over human rulers and kingdoms. This is the unifying theme of Dan. 1–6 (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

The Babylonian Empire is divided into provinces. Daniel is appointed ruler (cf. 3:2) of the province where the capital city is located. Joseph and Mordecai also rose as Jews to political power in a foreign land. See Gen. 41:37–44 (Joseph) and Esth. 8:1, 2 (Mordecai).

Although the narrow proportions might suggest an obelisk rather than a statue, the monument is called an “image.” It is probably a figure standing on a pedestal. The gold is probably plating, the fabrication of the image being much like that described in Is. 40:19; 41:7; Jer. 10:3–9. It reflects the enormous statue that Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream in ch. 2, except that it is entirely made of gold, as if Nebuchadnezzar is asserting that there will be no other kingdoms after his. It is not clear whether the image represents Nebuchadnezzar himself or one of his gods.

**He set it up.** Eight times in this chapter we are told that this is the image that Nebuchadnezzar set up, making it clear that it is merely an idol made by man, not a god with transcendent powers.

**the plain of Dura.** Probably about six miles (10 km) south of Babylon. Since it is set up on a plain in Babylon (lit. “Babel”) and has the purpose of unifying his diverse subjects, it recalls the tower of Babel in Gen. 11).

The precise responsibilities of these different provincial officials are not known. Five of the seven terms are of Persian origin, perhaps indicating that Daniel does not finish writing the account until after the beginning of Persian rule in 539 B.C. Leaders from across Nebuchadnezzar’s vast empire are assembled, making it clear that the unity of the empire is to be rooted in the common worship of this statue.

Of the six terms for musical instruments, the three translated “lyre,” “harp,” and “bagpipe” are borrowed from Greek. This is not surprising since the international exchange of musicians and musical instruments at royal courts has a long history. The presence of these three Greek terms in Daniel does not establish that the account was written after the time of Alexander the Great, as is sometimes argued. However, the diverse assortment of instruments may be an attempt to bring together different musical traditions from around the empire in this new centralized worship.
Furnaces or kilns were used in Babylon for firing bricks (Gen. 11:3). Execution by burning was not unknown (Jer. 29:22; cf. Herodotus 1:86; 4:69; 2 Macc. 7).

verse_quote: all the peoples, nations, and languages.
note: It seems as if Nebuchadnezzar’s idol has successfully revoked the curse on the tower of Babel.

See note on 2:2; here “Chaldeans” may indicate Babylonian nationality or that these men are diviners. The informers are prejudiced against the Jews (v. 12; cf. Esth. 3:5, 6), possibly because they are jealous of the privileged position held by Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (1:7 note). They charge them with rebellion and ingratitude toward Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel is presumably not present on this occasion.
From Nebuchadnezzar’s polytheistic perspective, there is no god capable of such deliverance. Unwittingly, Nebuchadnezzar challenges the power of the God of Israel (cf. 2 Kin. 18:33–35).

verse_quote: he will deliver ... But if not.
note: These verses express the central theme of the chapter. The idea is not that God will always protect His people from physical harm (Is. 43:1, 2). He may do that and certainly is able to. The central idea is that God’s people should be obedient to Him whatever the consequences., 18
This is likely hyperbole, meaning “as hot as possible.” It is ironic that the result is the death of Nebuchadnezzar’s own soldiers, while God protects His servants.
How Nebuchadnezzar recognizes the fourth person in the furnace as a divine being is not explained (v. 28 note). Perhaps the miraculous appearance is itself sufficient reason for the conclusion.

This is a title expressing God’s universal authority. As in v. 29 and 2:47, such a confession on the lips of a pagan is not an acknowledgment that Daniel’s Lord is the only God, but only that He is supreme over other gods (4:2, 17, 34). He still speaks of the Lord as “their God” (v. 28), not his. To a Jew, there is only one God (4:24–32; 5:18, 21; 7:18–27).

The “angel” may be identified with the Angel of the Lord (Gen. 16:7); if so, it is a visible manifestation of God Himself (Ex. 3:2). God promised His presence when Israel walked through fire, and in this incident He shows Himself faithful to that promise (Is. 43:1–3).

This final incident in the Book of Daniel associated with Nebuchadnezzar must be placed late in the king’s forty-three-year reign when his building projects are complete and his power is at its height (cf. vv. 4, 30). He represents the most powerful kingdom on earth (vv. 10–12 note) as being opposed to the rule of the Most High God. Babylonian records of long periods of absence and blasphemous acts by King Nabonidus (ruled 556 to 539 B.C.; 5:1 note) resemble in some ways Daniel’s account of Nebuchadnezzar. Another composition called the “Prayer of Nabonidus” has been discovered among the Dead Sea Scrolls, documents hidden before A.D. 70 by a Jewish community at Qumran and found in 1947. This “Prayer” is also similar to what Daniel says about Nebuchadnezzar. Nabonidus is separated from society for seven years and restored with the help of a Jewish exile after confession of his sins. However, his affliction is described as a form of skin disease rather than mental illness.

See notes on 2:47; 3:26. The narrative begins at the end of the story with the letter that Nebuchadnezzar writes to all peoples, nations, and languages, the same group gathered before the golden image in ch. 3. The signs and wonders mentioned here include the deliverance of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the previous chapter. What is different is that now these have been done “for me.” For the first time, Nebuchadnezzar himself becomes a witness to God.
Nebuchadnezzar’s confession in this verse and in vv. 34, 35 communicates the central theme of the book of Daniel, namely, the absolute sovereignty of the God of Israel.
See notes on 1:20; 2:2., 7

See note on 1:7. In the narrative frame, written after the events described in the chapter, Nebuchadnezzar calls him by his Judean name, Daniel, while in the conversations reported from the past he calls him Belteshazzar.

**the spirit of the holy gods.** The Holy Spirit is the immediate author of the extraordinary power of Daniel to know and to interpret secrets (2:19 note). Nebuchadnezzar’s words agree with this, although he may be thinking of another god known to him rather than the God of Daniel.

See Ezek. 31 for an extensive description of Assyria using the imagery of a tree. Similar imagery is used both of righteous and wicked individuals and nations Pss. 1:3; 37:35; 52:8; 92:12; Jer. 11:16, 17; 17:8.

This resembles the tower of Babel in Gen. 11:4. The term “heaven” is a key term in this chapter. Although Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom reaches from earth to heaven, heaven condemns his pride and reminds him that his power and even his sanity are gifts from God. Many allusions have also been noted in this section to the Garden of Eden in Gen. 1–3.

A name used of an angel only here in the OT. It alludes to the fact that God’s envoys constantly observe the activities of men and are ready to intervene to carry out the Lord’s judgment (cf. Zech. 1:8–17).

Though Nebuchadnezzar is judged and humbled, he is not destroyed.

**bound with a band of iron and bronze.** This symbolizes the bondage of Nebuchadnezzar’s insanity.

The mental illness in which a person imagines himself to be an animal is called “zoanthropy” (a compound of the Greek words for “animal” and “man”). The one who thinks of himself in godlike terms has lost his very humanity.

**let seven periods of time pass over him.** This means seven periods of unspecified duration (cf. vv. 23, 25), such as seasons, years, or months. The number seven represents completeness in the Bible, so this is a complete period of judgment.
With this statement, much like Nathan’s to David (2 Sam. 12:7), Daniel applies the dream to Nebuchadnezzar.

verse_quote: your dwelling shall be with the beasts.
note:
With graphic detail, Daniel explains how Nebuchadnezzar’s mind will fail. He will be deprived of his throne, and he will lose his dignity as a human being created to rule animals and not to imitate them.

**the Most High rules.** The purpose of Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation is to compel him to recognize God’s sovereignty.

verse_quote: your kingdom shall be confirmed for you.
note:
Nebuchadnezzar is promised that in spite of the severity and length of his illness, he will regain his throne when he acknowledges God’s sovereignty.

**Heaven rules.** This is the first time in the Bible where “heaven” is used as a substitute for “God” (4:37). Cf. Matt. 5:3 with Luke 6:20.

verse_quote: let my counsel be acceptable to you.
note: The dream represents a warning. If Nebuchadnez­zar heeds the dream and humbles himself, the events that he has foreseen need not come to pass. But Nebuchadnezzar is unrepentant.

verse_quote: the roof of his royal palace.
note: From this vantage point, Nebuchadnezzar can see the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Wonders of the Ancient World, and the outer wall of Babylon, which is wide enough to drive several chariots along the top. It is not surprising that such a view feeds his pride.

The Lord demonstrates in Nebuchadnezzar’s life that He is able to humble the proud and to exalt the humble, leading Nebuchadnezzar to acknowledge His greatness. The persecutor of God’s people and the destroyer of Jerusalem is put in his place. Although Nebuchadnezzar confesses God’s sovereignty, he does not confess a belief that the God of Israel is the only God., 35

**4:37 King of heaven.** This unique title brings together the theme of the chapter: the rule of God from heaven (vv. 3, 26 and notes).

The name “Belshazzar” means “Bel, protect the king” (not to be confused with “Belteshazzar,” the Babylonian name given to Daniel; 1:7 note). From Babylonian sources we know that Belshazzar was placed in charge of affairs in Babylon while his father, Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, spent extensive periods of time at Tema in Arabia. The Babylonians were famous for their lavish feasts. The events of this chapter take place in 539 B.C., the year of Babylon’s fall to the Persians, many years after the death of Nebuchadnezzar in 563 B.C.

Under the influence of wine, Belshazzar commits a sacrilegious act.

**his father.** The immediate father of Belshazzar was Nabonidus, not Nebuchadnezzar. It is not unusual in Hebrew for the terms “father” (vv. 11, 13, 18) and “son” (v. 22) to be used as equivalents for “predecessor” and “successor” (text notes).
The temple vessels are defiled, not only by being put to profane use, but also by being used to honor the false gods of Babylon.
Here they are clearly visible to all, though not easily understood.
Literally, “the knots of his joints were loosened,” which may mean that he also loses control of his bodily functions.

verse_quote: the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers.
note:
See notes on 1:20; 2:2; cf. 2:27; 4:7.

**shows me its interpretation.** Once again, a king requires Daniel’s assistance to understand a message from God meant for him (2:5 note).

**purple.** Purple dye was fabulously expensive in antiquity, so only the wealthiest individuals could afford to wear clothing in this color.

**third ruler.** That is, close in power to Nabonidus and Belshazzar (5:1 note). “Third ruler” is an official designation of a high office, not necessarily the literal third in line to the throne.

It is unlikely that this is a wife of Belshazzar, since she is already present at the banquet (vv. 2, 3). Probably she is to be identified as the queen mother, one of very few women to have significant power in ancient royal courts (cf. 1 Kin. 15:3; 2 Kin. 11:1–3; 24:12; Jer. 13:18).

verse_quote: the spirit of the holy gods.
note: See note on 4:8. It is not surprising that the queen mother is more familiar with Daniel’s life and prominence than is Belshazzar. Daniel is in his eighties by this time (539 B.C.) He was brought to Babylon as a young man sixty-six years before (605 B.C.; 1:1 note).

This divine endowment can be understood as the presence of God’s Spirit in an individual or simply as the possession of a remarkable spirit characteristic of that individual.

**Belteshazzar.** See note on 1:7.

verse_quote: one of the exiles of Judah.
note: Belshazzar’s address to Daniel is designed to remind Daniel of his proper place in the Babylonian power structure. He ignores Daniel’s role in the time of Nebuchadnezzar and the queen mother’s positive assessment of him.
See note on v. 7.

verse_quote: Let your gifts be for yourself.
note: Daniel’s response omits the usual deferential forms of address that are customary in the Babylonian court. He may be rejecting Belshazzar’s offer of reward because he is conscious that it is only by God’s mercy that he is able to respond to the king’s request, and he does not want to use his God-given role as a means of personal profit (cf. Gen. 14:23; 1 Sam. 9:7 note). But why then does he accept them earlier (2:48) and later (v. 29)? Some interpreters believe he is here avoiding royal pressure to modify the ominous message (Num. 22:18; Mic. 3:5, 11). Or perhaps Daniel already knows the message that he is about to interpret: that Belshazzar has no power to deliver the gifts he is promising, since on the same night Daniel gives the interpretation he will lose his kingdom and his life.
See note on v. 2. In contrast to Nebuchadnezzar, who was humbled and then returned to power, Belshazzar has not humbled himself.
This statement summarizes the book’s theology (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

See note on v. 2.

**though you knew all this.** Because the king has even less excuse for his pride than his father, Nebuchadnezzar, the time of mercy is past (contrast a different case in 1 Tim. 1:13).
The writing on the wall is God’s answer to the arrogant challenge presented by Belshazzar’s pride and his defiance of the God who showed His existence and sovereignty in the time of Nebuchadnezzar.
Aramaic, like Hebrew, is usually written without vowels, so this very short inscription is ambiguous to the witnesses.

The Aramaic word can be a verb meaning “numbered” or a noun meaning “mina,” a unit of money. Daniel reads it as the verb to signify that the length of Belshazzar’s reign has been determined by God and is about to end (Jer. 50:18).
This word is also either a verb or a noun. Daniel reads it as a verb meaning “weighed,” signifying that Belshazzar has failed to measure up to God’s standards of righteousness.

This word, the singular of “parsin,” sounds like the Aramaic word for Persia and means “divided.” If those present at the banquet understand the three terms as nouns indicating various decreasing units of money—_mina,_ or sixty shekels; _tekel_, one shekel; _peres,_ a half (i.e., “divided”) shekel—it is not surprising that they cannot understand the inscription.

**Medes and Persians.** See Introduction: Date and Occasion.
Like Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar honors Daniel (2:48), but unlike his predecessor, he does not honor Daniel’s God (2:46, 47). Given the prophecy, it is an empty reward.

It is not known just how Belshazzar died. However, the Greek historians Herodotus and Xenophon report that Babylon was taken in a surprise attack by the Persians while the Babylonians were engaged in reveling and dancing.

It has long been alleged that this and other references to Darius the Mede in the book of Daniel (6:1, 6, 9, 25, 28; 9:1; 11:1) are historical errors. For this discussion, see note on 6:1.

**sixty-two.** The mina probably weighed sixty shekels. This, with the shekel and two half-shekels (v. 25 note), comes to sixty-two; since this is Dari­us’s age, the mina might be a reference to him in the prophecy.

See note on 5:31. Darius the Mede is not referred to in surviving historical sources outside the Bible, and there is no interval between Belshazzar and Nabonidus (5:1 note) and the accession of Cyrus of Persia. Commentators have suggested several identifications for “Darius the Mede”: (1) a throne name for Cyrus, the founder of the Persian Empire (v. 28 note); (2) a title; (3) a designation for Gobryas, a general who defected from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus and later captured Babylon. Cyrus made Gobryas governor over the territories the Persians took from the Babylonians.

**satraps.** See note on 3:2. One of their responsibilities is overseeing the collection and delivery of tribute, which provides ample opportunity for corruption.

verse_quote: an excellent spirit was in him.

note: Unintentionally, Daniel’s adversaries affirm not only his moral integrity but also the visible nature of his piety and commitment to the God of Israel.

The false implication is that Daniel concurs with the proposal. These officials are hypocritical in their seeming devotion to Darius. Their scheme is an attempt to manipulate him for their own designs.

**any god or man ... except to you.** Darius sees the proposal as more political than religious, and serves to consolidate his authority over newly conquered territories. It is a more subtle version of Nebuchadnezzar’s edict in ch. 3.

verse_quote: the law of the Medes and the Persians.
note: The unchangeableness of their law is attested in extrabiblical writings as well as in the book of Esther. It is always possible for the king to issue a counter-edict, but it means a loss of face for the king. The effect of the decree is to create a conflict for Daniel between allegiance to God and obedience to human government.

Daniel is fulfilling Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple, which anticipated those in exile praying toward Jerusalem from the land of their exile and asking the Lord to show them favor (1 Kin. 8:46–50).

**down on his knees.** In Scripture, standing is the regular posture in prayer (1 Chr. 23:30; Neh. 9:2–5), while kneeling, a mark of humility, occurs in circumstances of particular solemnity (1 Kin. 8:54; Ezra 9:5; Ps. 95:6; Luke 22:41; Acts 7:60; 9:40).

**as he had done previously.** Evidently Daniel’s prayer habits are public knowledge, which makes him an easy target.

verse_quote: Did you not sign an injunction.
note: Before they accuse Daniel, the satraps ask the king to confirm his edict, to make it harder for him to avoid its force when he has to condemn Daniel.

verse_quote: one of the exiles from Judah.
note: This ethnic identification of Daniel perhaps indicates prejudice toward the Jews on the part of the other officials (3:8); it underlines his lowly origins rather than his current position of responsibility and power.

verse_quote: set his mind to deliver Daniel.
note: Darius immediately perceives that he has been victimized by the intrigue of his own officials in order to trap Daniel. His loyalty to Daniel remains unshaken.
Against his own will, Darius is forced to comply with the decree that he issued. Darius can do nothing to help Daniel, yet he asks that Daniel’s God intervene on behalf of His faithful servant.

verse_quote: sealed it with his own signet.
note: Signet rings and cylinder seals were used by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Persians. The ring or cylinder was pressed into soft clay to leave the mark of the owner of the seal. Breaking seals was a violation of the law, and in this case an unbroken seal ensures that no one intervenes to rescue Daniel.
At the earliest possible moment, Darius goes to discover Daniel’s fate.

Possibly, although not necessarily in the context, the Angel of the Lord. See note on 3:28.

**I was found blameless.** Daniel’s name means “God is my judge” and here it is proved true: God vindicates him by protecting him from the lions. It appears that Daniel has passed a more peaceful night in the lions’ den than the king did surrounded by all of the luxuries of royalty.

Darius can rescue Daniel without violating the decree since its demands have been fulfilled.

**no kind of harm.** Cf. 3:25.

verse_quote: those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought.
note: Under ancient Near Eastern law, people who brought false charges against another suffer the same fate they had sought for the accused (see Deut. 19:16–21). As part of covenantal responsibility, the verdict affects the families of the accusers as well as men themselves. Their experience with the lions is the exact opposite of Daniel’s, proving that the divine Judge concurs with the verdict of the earthly king.

Cf. 2:47; 3:28, 29; 4:2, 3, 34–37; 5:18–29. As in the previous narratives, God displays His sovereign control of nature and history, kingdoms, and kings. The decree is an eloquent testimony to “the living God” and His indestructible kingdom. It is an official acknowledgment of Daniel’s God, although it does not necessarily reflect personal faith on the part of Darius.

God’s favor sustains Daniel and preserves his authority all the way through the exile until the Babylonian Empire is replaced by the Persians. Daniel’s whole life is metaphorically spent in a den of lions, yet God protects him.

**Darius ... Cyrus.** On the relationship between Darius and Cyrus, see note on 6:1. Darius the Mede has been interpreted by some as one and the same as Cyrus the Persian, based on a translation of a conjunctive particle in Aramaic being explanatory (even though it is usually translated as “and”). In this case, the verse would be best translated as “So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius _that is_ (or _even_) in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” There is precedence for such a construction in 1 Chr. 5:26, “So that the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, _that is_ the spirit of Tiglath-pileser.”

See note on 5:1. Belshazzar’s administration under Nabonidus may have begun at the same time as the accession of his father (556 B.C.) or a few years later. In either case, the visions of chs. 7 and 8 take place chronologically between the events of chs. 4 and 5, in the days when the Babylonians ruled the world.

Four is the number of completeness in the Bible, so the four winds of heaven represent winds blowing from all four points of the compass, rather than a danger from any particular direction.

**great sea.** The sea is a common figure for the restlessness and dangerous turmoil of sinful men and nations (see v. 17; cf. Is. 17:12, 13; 57:20). It is also the home of evil monsters such as Leviathan (Ps. 74:13, 14).

These four “beasts” may represent four kingdoms (vv. 17, 23) or, like the four winds of heaven (v. 2), they may represent all future kingdoms. The identification here corresponds closely to the four kingdoms of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in ch. 2. For discussion of the identification of the four kingdoms, see note on 2:37–40 and Introduction: Date and Occasion.

The “lion” with “eagles’ wings” is an appropriate symbol for the Babylonian Empire (cf. Jer. 50:44; Ezek. 17:3, 12). Winged lions with human faces are common in Babylonian art and are placed at the entrances of important public buildings in Daniel’s era. It is also an unclean mixture of bird and beast.

**wings were plucked off.** Perhaps this is a reference to Nebuchadnezzar’s humiliation and later restoration after a seven-year period of insanity (ch. 4).

The second kingdom is symbolized as a “beast” with a voracious appetite. If it represents Medo-Persia, the raised side may represent the superior status of Persia, and the “three ribs” Persia’s conquests over Lydia (546 B.C.), Babylon (539 B.C.), and Egypt (525 B.C.). See note on 8:3.

The third empire is symbolized by the “leopard,” known for its quickness. Alexander the Great (356–323 B.C.) conquered the Persian Empire with great speed. Alexander died suddenly at age thirty-three, and the empire he established was divided into four parts (Macedonia under Cassander, Thrace and Asia Minor under Lysimachus, Syria under Seleucus, and Egypt under Ptolemy). However, many other empires have also been militarily swift and fierce, so the identification of the leopard with Alexander, though likely, remains uncertain.

This last “beast” cannot be identified with any earthly animal. It is exceedingly powerful and terrifying, with great iron teeth that crush its enemies. Many interpreters believe that this last beast symbolizes Rome, the kingdom that ultimately assimilates the various parts of the divided Greek kingdom.

**it had ten horns.** The “ten horns” have been thought to symbolize ten kings or kingdoms associated with the Roman Empire (v. 24). Some interpreters suggest that a second phase of the fourth kingdom, a revived Roman Empire, is to be expected. According to Daniel’s vision, the ten horns will come from the fourth beast—the fourth kingdom—at once or one after the other (2:44 note; cf. Rev. 13:1–10; 17:3, 12).

The ten horns are prior in time to the “little horn” that uproots three of them, symbolizing another phase of the fourth kingdom. Many interpreters suggest that the little horn in some way represents the Antichrist (2 Thess. 2:3, 4, 8). If so, this is the first reference in Scripture to the Antichrist. However, in the absence of any clear direction from the interpreting angel in what follows, all identifications must remain tentative.

verse_quote: the Ancient of Days took his seat.
note:
The title “Ancient of Days” occurs in the Bible only in this chapter (vv. 13, 22). It is a designation for God on the throne and divine judgment.

**white as snow ... like pure wool.** His clothing symbolizes radiant purity, while his hair represents the wisdom that comes with great age.

**his throne ... its wheels.** The depiction of God’s throne resembles Ezekiel’s vision of the throne chariot of God, underlining the theme of judgment (Ezek. 1:15–28).

A contrast is drawn between the complete destruction of the fourth kingdom and the measure of continuance granted the preceding kingdoms as their people and customs were absorbed into the succeeding kingdoms., 12

Elsewhere in the OT, only God comes on the clouds (Ps. 104:3; Is. 19:1). Accordingly, the “son of man” originates in heaven and comes by divine initiative.

**one like a son of man.** The equivalent phrase is used for Daniel in 8:17 and many times for Daniel’s contemporary Ezekiel (e.g., Ezek. 2:1, 3, 6). In contrast to the previous “beasts” who have misruled the earth, the son of man will rule as God intended before humanity’s fall (Gen. 1:26–28; Ps. 8:4–6). The expression “Son of Man” is used sixty-nine times in the Synoptic Gospels and twelve times in the gospel of John to refer to Christ. It is the title Jesus most often used of Himself. Linguistically, the Aramaic phrase here translated as “son of man” means either “a human being” as opposed to the preceding “beasts” or a divine being. In light of the application of the phrase to Jesus, both are likely in view. Daniel’s “son of man” is a divine-human ruler, specifically the God-man, Jesus Christ.

The “son of man” is Christ, the Messiah, and the word for “serve” implies acts of worship. Jesus referred this passage to Himself, causing the religious leaders of His day to accuse Him of blasphemy (Matt. 26:64, 65; Mark 14:62–64).

**an everlasting dominion.** He is given God’s sovereignty and exercises the rule symbolized by the stone that fell in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (2:34, 35, 44, 45).

verse_quote: he ... made known to me the interpretation of the things.
note: In contrast to the speculations of commentators, the angel tells Daniel exactly what the vision means. In other words, all of our interpretations of the vision need to end up declaring the content of vv. 17, 18.

verse_quote: These four great beasts are four kings.
note: Interestingly, the angel identifies the animals as kings, not kingdoms. He does not explain who these kings are, which suggests that identifying them is not essential for grasping the meaning of the vision.

verse_quote: the saints of the Most High.
note: See vv. 21, 22, 25, 27. The “saints” are not angels, but believers in God who will share in Christ’s kingdom (Matt. 19:28; 1 Cor. 6:1–3; 2 Tim. 2:12; Rev. 22:5). The main point of the vision is that in spite of the constant presence of antagonistic rulers and powers (Bab­ylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and many other nation states and empires), the saints of the Most High will finally triumph alongside the Son of Man.

verse_quote: I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast.
note: Daniel’s attention is drawn to the identity of the fourth beast; however, the interpreting angel’s answer will end up returning to the point made in vv. 17, 18.

Daniel is given some additional information about the hostility of the little horn, possibly the Antichrist (v. 8), toward the people of God (cf. Rev. 13:7). However, since many antichrists precede the Antichrist (1 John 2:18), it is not surprising that several historical rulers such as Antiochus IV Epiphanes have oppressed the saints in similar ways. The message of the vision is relevant to God’s people in many contexts before the time of the end.

verse_quote: until the Ancient of Days came.
note: Although the Antichrist will prevail for a time against God’s people, in the end he will fall under the judgment of God (Zech. 14:1–4; Rev. 13:7–17; 19:20).

verse_quote: for a time, times, and half a time.
note: The word “time” is the same word used in 4:16 and 4:23, and, as it does there, it may mean one year. Some interpreters take this verse to refer to the last half of the seventieth week of 9:24–27. Others do not assign a specific duration to the expression but take it to be a period of time that is shortened because God intervenes. It is “three and a half times” rather than a full period of judgment, which would be “seven times” (see 4:16).

verse_quote: the saints of the Most High.
note: See note on v. 18. The final triumph of the saints through enduring persecution is the central theme of the chapter.

Daniel resumes writing in Hebrew for the last five chapters. He used Aramaic in 2:4–7:28 (2:4 note).

**8:1 In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar.** That is, two years after Daniel’s dream in ch. 7 (7:1 note).

Daniel has a visionary journey like that of Ezekiel (Ezek. 3:10–15).

**in Susa the capital.** In Daniel’s time, Susa is the capital of Elam, about 230 miles (370 km) east of Babylon. It is not clear whether Elam is independent or aligned with Babylon or Media. Later, however, as one of three royal cities, Susa becomes the diplomatic and administrative center of the Persian Empire (cf. Neh. 1:1; Esth. 1:2).

**the Ulai canal.** This canal near Susa connects two rivers that flow into the Persian Gulf.

According to v. 20, the ram and its horns represent the kings of the Medo-Persian Empire. Unlike in ch. 7, the interpreting angel makes the historical meaning of this vision clear.

**one was higher than the other, and ... came up last.** Medo-Persian history clarifies the symbolism. The Medes became independent of Assyria after 612 B.C. The Persians were under the control of the Medes, but eventually rose to prominence when Cyrus of Anshan defeated his Median overlord in 550 B.C. Cyrus (who reigned 559–530 B.C.) called himself “King of the World.”

verse_quote: charging westward and northward and southward.
note:
That is, his back is toward the east from where he came (Is. 41:2). Cyrus first took Asia Minor, then northern and southern Mesopotamia. Subsequent rulers extended Medo-Persian control far to the east.

**became great.** The Persian Empire became larger than any previous empire in ancient Near Eastern history.

verse_quote: from the west ... the goat had a conspicuous horn.
note:
According to v. 21, the goat represents Greece and the large horn between his eyes is the first king. The symbolism clearly depicts the rise of the Greek Empire under Alexander the Great (356–323 B.C.).

**across ... the whole earth, without touching the ground.** These words describe the amazing speed and extent of Alexander’s conquests (7:6 note). In only three years he defeated the powerful Persian Empire.

Alexander’s empire quickly exceeded the Persian Empire in size. By 327 B.C., Alexander moved east into what is today Afghanistan and then on to the Indus River in modern-day Pakistan.

**the great horn was broken.** Alexander died in Babylon at the age of thirty-three.

**instead of it there came up four conspicuous horns.** According to v. 22, these horns are four kingdoms that emerged from Alexander’s empire but were inferior to it in strength. After a time of internal struggle, four of Alexander’s generals took portions of the Greek Empire as their own kingdoms. See note on 7:6.

According to v. 23, this “little horn” symbolizes a wicked ruler who will arise in one of the four Greek kingdoms after a long interval of time (“at the latter end of their kingdom”). The descriptions of the actions of this ruler (vv. 9–14; 23–25) indicate that he is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, ruler of the Seleucid kingdom from 175 to 164 B.C. This horn must be distinguished from the “little one” of 7:8 if that chapter refers to the Roman period and not the Greek.

**toward the glorious land.** That is, toward Palestine.

The “host of heaven” or the “stars” (cf. Jer. 33:22) symbolize the people of God (cf. 12:3; Gen. 15:5) or a heavenly army (Is. 14:13; also see 2 Macc. 9:10). The attack against the people of God amounts to an attack against heaven itself.

**some of the host and some of the stars it threw down to the ground.** This is a symbolic depiction of the severe persecution of God’s people under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who attempted to abolish their traditional worship and way of life and forcibly Hellenize them (cf. vv. 11:21–35 and 1 Macc. 1:10–64 for additional details; cf. also Introduction to the Intertestamental Period).

verse_quote: as great as the Prince of the host.
note:
The “Prince” is to be understood as God (see v. 25 where the designation is “Prince of princes”). Antiochus IV took the name Epiphanes (“God manifest”) and thought of himself as a manifestation of Zeus.

**the regular burnt offering was taken away.** See vv. 12, 13 and 11:31. Antiochus IV summarily forbade all ceremonies and worship of God in the Jerusalem temple and the cities of Judah.

**the place of his sanctuary was overthrown.** Antiochus IV entered the Most Holy Place and plundered the silver and gold vessels. He erected an altar to the Olympian Zeus on the altar of God in the temple court and there sacrificed pigs (11:31 note).

The temple in Jerusalem was destroyed in Daniel’s own time because of the sins of God’s people; here Daniel is told that a similar cycle would occur again.

**throw truth to the ground.** Among his transgressions, Antiochus IV destroyed copies of Scripture (1 Macc. 1:56, 57).

**it will act and prosper.** The vision depicts the apparent success of the wicked acts of Antiochus IV, the little horn.

Compare the “vision of the evenings and the mornings” in v. 26. Some interpreters understand it simply as a reference to the evening and morning sacrifices as separate offerings (cf. Ex. 29:38–42). On this basis, it represents 1,150 days, for these paired evening and morning sacrifices are traditionally considered a single offering. Others understand it as simply an expression for 2,300 days. Since the persecutions by Antiochus IV could be linked with any one of a number of incidents beginning as early as 171 B.C. and ending with the rededication of the temple in 164 B.C., it is difficult to say which understanding of the phrase is to be preferred. The multiple of the number twenty-three may simply be symbolic for a fixed period as in extrabiblical apocalypses (cf. the sixty-nine [23 x 3] weeks in 9:25, 26). Calling them “evenings and mornings” recalls the days of creation in Gen. 1, whose order the little horn seems determined to destroy. It also suggests that God has a precise schedule for the period of suffering of His saints, even though humans cannot decode His plans.

**Then the sanctuary shall be restored.** The temple was cleansed and rededicated under the leadership of Judas Maccabeus in December 164 B.C. (11:34 note; cf. Zech. 9:13–17).
This angel is mentioned four times in Scripture (9:21; Luke 1:19, 26). The name means “mighty one of God” or “God is mighty.”

See note on 7:13. The “strong man of God” is speaking to this distinguished “mortal.”

**the time of the end.** See also v. 19 (“the appointed time of the end”). This expression is not necessarily eschatological (referring to the end of history). It occurs in 11:27, 35 in contexts that are clearly not eschatological. Here it may refer to the end of the persecutions of Antiochus IV.
The time of “the indignation” may refer to the period of God’s judgment on Israel during its subjection to the Babylonians, Persians, and Greeks.
See notes on vv. 3, 4.
See notes on vv. 5, 8.
See note on v. 8.

See notes on vv. 9–14. Some interpreters perceive the Antichrist in the descriptions of the “little horn” of this chapter. Antiochus IV is viewed as a type pointing forward to a later manifestation of satanic power in the person of the Antichrist.

This is a reference to God (v. 11 note).

**by no human hand.** Antiochus IV died of a physical or nervous disorder in 164 B.C. For accounts of his death, see 1 Macc. 6:1–16 and 2 Macc. 9.

The term “seal” can mean to authenticate or certify something, or to close up for confidentiality and safekeeping. The second sense seems best in this context (6:17 note).

**it refers to many days from now.** The words “from now” have been supplied by the translators. The conquests of Alexander (333–323 B.C.) occurred more than two centuries after Daniel’s vision (c. 550 B.C.). The activities of Antiochus IV were about a century and a half after Alexander (171–164 B.C.).

Daniel does not fully understand the vision, but he recognizes that it depicts a lengthy period of suffering for his people in the future. As the other prophets did, he identifies with the suffering of his people (cf. Ezek. 3:14, 15).

**went about the king’s business.** Daniel continues to seek the welfare of the earthly city where God placed him.

Daniel recounts the revelation he received concerning the prophecy of Jeremiah about the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation (Jer. 25:11, 12; 29:10). Significantly, the revelation follows Daniel’s prayer confessing the sinfulness of God’s people and the justice of Jerusalem’s desolation, and his seeking the favor of God for the restoration of the city and the temple.

**9:1 the first year of Darius the son of Ahas­uerus.** See note on 6:1. The word “Ahasuerus” (not the same person mentioned in Esth. 1:1) may be a royal title rather than a personal name. The first year of Darius was 539 B.C.

verse_quote: the desolations of Jerusalem ... seventy years.
note: Interpreters differ on the dates of the beginning and ending of the seventy-year period, and on whether it is to be understood as a round number for a human lifetime or exactly seventy years. Some date the period from 586 B.C. (the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar) to 516 B.C., when the restoration of the temple was completed under Zerubbabel (Ezra 6:13–18). Others date the beginning of the period to the year of Daniel’s own captivity (605 B.C.; 1:1 note), which suggests that Daniel recognizes the end of the seventy years is imminent. Either way, it is clear that Daniel’s prayer is motivated by reading Jeremiah’s prophecy, especially in view of the fall of Babylon, which Jeremiah anticipated. Daniel sees that two things are to happen according to Jeremiah (25:11, 12; 29:10–14): the fall of Babylon and the restoration of the people to the Promised Land. The first has happened at the time of Daniel’s prayer, but the second has not. Therefore, Daniel beseeches the Lord to accomplish the second. God responds to the prayer with an answer to this and even more.
These are signs of repentance and mourning over sin.

Daniel’s prayer is rooted in a covenantal understanding of the Lord’s relation to His people (blessing for obedience, cursing for disobedience, especially vv. 5, 7, 11, 12, 14; cf. Lev. 26:14–45; Deut. 28:15–68; 30:1–5). For a similar prayer, see Neh. 9. The prayer has four parts: (1) worship (v. 4); (2) a confession of sin (vv. 5–11); (3) recognition of God’s justice in His judgment on sin (vv. 11–14); and (4) a plea for God’s mercy based on concern for His name, kingdom, and will (vv. 15–19). The prayer is grounded on God’s promises (v. 2) and offered in a spirit of contrition and humility (v. 3). It is a model for the appropriate elements of effective prayer.
See note on 8:16. Gabriel’s arrival is proof that Daniel’s prayer has been heard and his request for the Lord’s favor has been approved.

The interpretation of these verses is disputed at many points. There are two fundamental approaches to the interpretation of the “weeks” (lit. “sevens”): as symbolic periods of time or as literal periods of time. In the symbolic view, the seventy years of punishment (v. 2) are multiplied seven times in accordance with the covenantal curses (Lev. 26:18, 21, 24, 28). Jubilees_,_ a Jewish book from the intertestamental period, also structures the whole of history into periods of 490 years. Adherents of the literal view fall into three categories. As with other prophecies in Daniel, some commentators interpret the verses with reference to the time of Antiochus IV. Other interpreters may be divided into two categories: (1) those who interpret the passage as having its primary focus on events associated with the first coming of Christ and shortly thereafter (first-coming view); (2) those who interpret the passage as having reference to events associated with both the first and second comings of Christ, necessitating an unstated time interval between the two (second-coming view). Within each of these broad categories, individual interpreters differ on specific details.

**9:24 Seventy weeks.** Most interpreters view the units of “seventy weeks” (lit., “seventy sevens”) as representing 490 years (9:24–27 note). These so-called seventy weeks of years are then divided into three subunits of 49 years (“seven weeks,” v. 25); 434 years (“sixty-two weeks,” v. 26); and 7 years (“one week,” v. 27). Interpreters differ over whether these subunits are to be viewed as a continuous sequence or as having time intervals between them. More important, the main point of Gabriel’s answer is that Daniel’s request for God to deal with the sin and wickedness of the Lord’s people will be answered in the affirmative, though not immediately. The seventy years of which Jeremiah spoke and which are now nearing an end will be extended into a longer period of “seventy times seven” years (cf. Matt. 18:22). Notice that six purposes are to be achieved within the “seventy weeks.” These are divided into three pairs: (1) the first and second purposes deal with the sin of the old covenant community; (2) the third and fourth purposes deal with the inauguration of the messianic period; and (3) the fifth and sixth purposes express that everything will be fulfilled.

verse_quote: the going out of the word.
note:
The Hb. term translated “word” may mean either “word” or “command.” This ambiguity has given rise to multiple interpretations for the beginning of the “seventy weeks”: (1) Some interpreters understand it to be the decree issued by Artaxerxes I in the seventh year of his reign (457 B.C.; Ezra 7:12–26). Forty-nine years later (408 B.C.), the streets and wall around Jerusalem were completed (v. 25). (2) Other commentators understand the “seventy weeks” as beginning in 587 B.C., the time of Jeremiah’s prediction (his “word”) that Jerusalem would be rebuilt (Jer. 31:38; 32:15, 37, 44). Forty-nine years later would be 538 B.C., the year that Cyrus permitted the Jews to fulfill Jeremiah’s prophecy by returning to Palestine (Ezra 1:1–4). (3) Since ancient times, many interpreters have also understood the “seventy weeks” symbolically. Proponents of this view note a sabbatical pattern in the six purposes of the seventy weeks (9:24 note), culminating in the work of the Messiah described in the final week.

**to the coming of an anointed one, a prince.** Advocates of interpretation (1) in the previous note understand “anointed one” to be a reference to Jesus. Linking the “seven weeks” (forty-nine years) and the “sixty-two weeks” (434 years) as a continuous sequence yields 483 years, from 457 B.C. to A.D. 27, or approximately the beginning of Christ’s three-year public ministry. Others take the 483 years to begin with the “command” of Artaxerxes I in the twentieth year of his reign (444 B.C.; Neh. 2:1), instead of the seventh year of his reign (Ezra 7:12–26) in 457 B.C. Using a 360-day lunar year (as in the Jewish calendar), this approach reaches a date for the crucifixion in A.D. 33. This date for the crucifixion is possible but not certain. Advocates of interpretation (3) in the previous note also believe Jesus to be the “anointed one,” though the specific chronology in this verse is understood symbolically. Advocates of interpretation (2) in the previous note understand “anointed one” to refer to Cyrus (also called the Lord’s “anointed”; Is. 45:1). This view separates the “seven weeks” and the “sixty-two weeks.” The “seven weeks” elapse between the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. and the decree of Cyrus in 538 B.C. The “sixty-two weeks” (434 years) is the time when the city is to be rebuilt, somewhere between 538 B.C. and A.D. 70 (Jerusalem’s destruction at the hands of the Roman general Titus). This view requires a time interval between the two periods of “weeks.”

verse_quote: after the sixty-two weeks, an anointed one shall be cut off.
note:
Many interpreters understand this to refer to the crucifixion of Christ. According to interpretation (2) in the first note on 9:25, the “anointed one” of v. 26 is Christ, and the “anointed one” of v. 25 is Cyrus.

**the people of the prince.** Some interpreters think that the assailants are the armies of Titus who destroyed Jerusalem in A.D. 70. Some adherents of the second-coming view (9:24–27 note) argue that while the assailants are the armies of Titus, the “prince” himself is the Antichrist. This identification provides a transition to the second-coming interpretation of v. 27. However, it seems more plausible that the references to “the anointed one” and “the coming prince” in v. 26 both point back to the “coming anointed prince” in v. 25. In that view, the prince is Jesus, and the people who destroyed Jerusalem are the Jews of His day, whose rejection of Christ led to the destruction of their own temple (see Luke 19:37–46).

verse_quote: he shall make a strong covenant with many for one week.
note:
Advocates of the first-coming view (9:24–27 note) understand that the “anointed one” will “make a strong covenant,” that is, live out his public ministry, atone for sin, and inaugurate the new righteousness promised in v. 24. In this view, the one who will make the strong covenant is none other than the God identified in Is. 9:6 as “Mighty God” (the Hb. words translated “strong” and “mighty” are related). Moreover, there are significant vocabulary overlaps between Is. 10:20–23 (another Messianic passage) and the language of this verse.Advocates of the second-coming view (9:24­–27 note) posit a time interval between vv. 26 and 27 and understand that the “prince” will “make a strong covenant.” The “prince” is identified as Antichrist, who will establish a covenant with the Jewish people regathered in the land of Israel during a “tribulation” period (12:1; Matt. 24:21; Rev. 7:14) of seven years (the seventieth “week”).

**an end to sacrifice.** According to advocates of the first-coming view (9:24–27 note), this refers to the termination of the OT sacrificial system brought about by the death of Christ. According to advocates of the second-coming view, this is a reference to the Antichrist’s prohibition of “sacrifice and offering” (perhaps standing for religious practice in general) by the regathered Jewish people after three-and-a-half years (Rev. 11:2; 12:6, 14) of the tribulation period.

**one who makes desolate.** This envisages a climactic abomination that results in the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. According to the first-coming view (9:24–27 note), this describes the cutting off of God’s appointed Messiah on the cross, which led to the destruction of Jerusalem that occurred in A.D. 70. According to the second-coming view, this passage describes a catastrophe that will come upon a rebuilt Jerusalem temple in connection with the activities of the Antichrist just before the second coming of Christ. Phrases similar to “an abomination that makes desolate” that occur in Dan. 8:13; 11:31; 12:11 (see notes), as well as 1 Macc. 1:54, are clearly references to the activities of Antiochus IV. Jesus referred to this “abomination” in His prophecy of events yet future in His own day (Matt. 24:15; Mark 13:14).

The prophet reveals a final vision concerning the future reign of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, but looking beyond his reign to another that culminates at the end of the age. The three chapters make up a single vision.

**10:1 the third year of Cyrus.** 537 B.C. See note on 1:21. The repatriated exiles returned to the land to rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–4; 3:8) but would soon have to cease their efforts temporarily (Ezra 4:24).

Daniel probably mourns because of the state of Jerusalem, and he voluntarily abstains from choice foods such as meat and wine to identify with the trials of his brothers and sisters in Judah (Neh. 1:4; Is. 61:3, 4; 64:8–12; 66:10).

Verses 5, 6 give a detailed description of an angel, perhaps the one who spoke to Gabriel (8:16), or Gabriel himself (9:21). His appearance is much like that of the glory of the Lord, which he reflects as one of the divine attendants (Ezek. 1:26–28; Rev. 1:12–16). For other references to angels, see Judg. 13:6; Ezek. 9:2, 3; 10:2; Luke 24:4.
See Is. 6:5; Luke 5:8.

verse_quote: no strength was left in me.
note: Daniel was overwhelmed even by the reflected form of divine glory. Yet the angel dealt with him gently, bringing him first to his hands and knees before enabling him to stand, and addressing him as a man greatly loved by God.

verse_quote: I have come because of your words.
note: The vision and revelation that Daniel receives comes as a direct response to his prayers.

verse_quote: The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me.
note:
This “prince” is an evil but powerful spiritual being (cf. Is. 24:21; Luke 11:14–26) who is influencing Persian rule.

**Michael.** A being depicted elsewhere in Scripture as a commander of the holy angels (Jude 9; Rev. 12:7; cf. 2 Kin. 6:15–17). Here is a glimpse of spiritual battles waged in heavenly places and affecting events on earth (cf. Eph. 6:12; Rev. 12:7–9). The power of fallen angels is limited by God, as is made clear here and elsewhere in Scripture (Job 1:12; 2:6). The “prince of the kingdom of Persia” could delay the angel who came to Daniel, but he could not prevent him from carrying out his mission.

See note on v. 13.

**the prince of Greece.** This angel affects the affairs of the Greek kingdom (v. 13 note). Although both Persia and Greece will rule over God’s people after the prophet’s lifetime, Daniel must understand that their power is limited by the power of God.

A metaphor for God’s knowledge and control of all history.

**none ... except Michael.** Michael’s interest to protect God’s people (v. 13 note; cf. 12:1) corresponds to the interest of the angelic messenger, who is directly concerned with God’s purposes.

verse_quote: in the first year of Darius the Mede.
note: Two years earlier (10:1 note), the angel who is speaking to Daniel gave assistance to Michael (10:13 note), perhaps in connection with the Persian decree to permit the Jews to return to their homeland. God’s people can be assured that they are not alone in their spiritual conflict.

The revelation given to Daniel in 11:2–12:4 is in three parts: 11:2–20 depicts in precise detail ancient Near Eastern history from the time of Daniel until the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes; 11:21–35 describes the rule of Antiochus IV; and 11:36–12:4 apparently describes the time of the Antichrist. In Is. 44:6, 7, the Lord asserts His ability to declare ahead of time what will happen in the future; here that power is displayed to encourage Daniel about the Lord’s sovereign control over every twist and turn of world history.

**11:2 three more kings.** They are Cambyses, 529–523 B.C.; Pseudo-Smerdis (Gaumata), 523–522 B.C.; and Darius I, 522–486 B.C.

**a fourth.** Xerxes I, 485–464 B.C., known in the OT as Ahasuerus.

**his riches.** See Esth. 1:4.

**against the kingdom of Greece.** Xerxes waged a number of campaigns against Greece beginning in 480 B.C., but he was defeated at the battle of Salamis.
Alexander the Great, 336–323 B.C. See notes on 7:6; 8:5, 8.
See notes on 7:6; 8:8.

Ptolemy I Soter, 322–285 B.C.

**one of his princes.** Seleucus I Nicator, 312–280 B.C. Seleucus broke with Ptolemy, became king of Babylon, and controlled territories from the Indus River in the east to Syria in the west.

These verses contain detailed predictions of relations between the king of the North (the Seleucid kingdom) and the king of the South (the Ptolemaic kingdom). The section concerns events involving Laodice and Berenice (vv. 6–9), the career of Antiochus III (vv. 10–19), and the reign of Seleucus IV (v. 20).

**11:6 the daughter of the king.** Berenice, the daughter of Ptolemy II Philadelphus, 285–246 B.C.

**to make an agreement.** A marriage alliance (about 250 B.C.) between Antiochus II Theos (261–246 B.C.) of Syria and Ptolemy II of Egypt.

**he and his arm shall not endure.** Laodice, the former wife of Antiochus II, led a conspiracy that resulted in the poisoning deaths of Berenice, Antiochus II, and their infant son.

Ptolemy III Euergetes, 246–221 B.C., the brother of Berenice (v. 6 note).

**enter the fortress.** Ptolemy III attacked the Seleucid kingdom, executed Laodice (see v. 6 note), and returned to Egypt with considerable booty.
Seleucus II Callinicus (246–226 B.C.), the son of Laodice, led an unsuccessful campaign against the Ptolemaic kingdom in 240 B.C.

Seleucus III Ceraunus, 226–223 B.C.; Antiochus III the Great, 223–187 B.C.

**shall wage war.** Antiochus III began to fight against the Ptolemies in 219 B.C. and for a time gained control of Palestine and western Syria.

**his fortress.** This probably refers to Raphia, a Ptolemaic fortress in southern Palestine, where a major battle was fought in 217 B.C.

Ptolemy IV Philopator, 221–203 B.C.

**against the king of the north.** Antiochus III. Antiochus suffered great losses, more than 14,000 men, at the battle of Raphia in 217 B.C.

In alliance with Philip V of Macedon, Antiochus III raised an even larger army to invade the Ptolemaic kingdom. Ptolemy IV died under mysterious circumstances and was succeeded by Ptolemy V Epiphanes, 203–181 B.C., his four-year-old son.
The victory of Antiochus III over the Egyptian general Scopas at Sidon in 198 B.C. marked the end of Ptolemaic rule in Palestine.
Palestine. See vv. 41, 45; 8:9.

verse_quote: it shall not stand or be to his advantage.
note: After Cleopatra was given in marriage to Ptolemy V by her father Antiochus III, she aligned herself with the Egyptian cause, seeking Roman help against her father’s attempt to take coastal cities in Asia Minor that were controlled by Egypt.

The Roman general Lucius Cornelius Scipio, who defeated Antiochus III in several battles and forced him to cede Asia Minor to Roman control (the Peace of Apamea, 188 B.C.). At this time the second son of Antiochus III, who became Antiochus IV Epiphanes, was taken hostage to Rome.

Seleucus IV Philopator, 187–175 B.C. (the older son of Antiochus III).

**tribute for the glory of the kingdom.** For an account of Heliodorus’s attempt to collect these taxes for Seleucus, see 2 Macc. 3:7–40.

Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 B.C.), who was not the legitimate successor of his brother Seleucus IV, since Seleucus IV had a son. See notes on 8:9–14. He is a particular focus of attention because of his persecution of the Jewish people.

verse_quote: even the prince of the covenant.
note: Perhaps this is a reference to the assassination in 171 B.C. of the high priest Onias III by supporters of Antiochus IV based in Jerusalem (see 2 Macc. 4:32–43).

Ptolemy VI Philometor, 181–146 B.C., son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra, and the nephew of Antiochus (v. 17 note).

**he shall not stand.** Antiochus IV defeated Ptolemy VI at Pelusium, on the border of Egypt (cf. 1 Macc. 1:16–19).

verse_quote: he shall return ... his heart shall be set against the holy covenant.
note: In response to intrigues in Jerusalem against his supporters, Antiochus IV plundered the temple when he returned from Egypt to Syrian Antioch (cf. 1 Macc. 1:20–28).
Antiochus IV invaded Egypt again in 168 B.C.

Roman armies under Gaius Popilius Laenas forced Antiochus IV to retreat from Egypt.

**take action against the holy covenant.** Antiochus IV determined to exterminate the Jewish religion. See note on 8:11.
The desecration of the temple in December 168 B.C. by Antiochus IV (cf. 1 Macc. 1:54, 59; 2 Macc. 6:2). See notes on 8:11; 9:27; 12:11.

verse_quote: the people who know their God.
note: Daniel speaks of those who opposed the Hellenizers and were ready to die for their faith (1 Macc. 1:60–63).

verse_quote: they shall receive a little help.
note: Possibly this is a reference to Mattathias, an elderly priest, and his five sons (John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar, and Jonathan) who waged a guerrilla war against the forced hellenization (imposition of Greek ways) of the Jews. Mattathias died in 166 B.C. His sons, known as the Maccabees, carried on the struggle. Victory was achieved under Judas Maccabeus in December 164 B.C., when the temple was cleansed and daily sacrifices were restored (1 Macc. 4:36–39).
See note on 8:17.

Certain details in 11:36–12:3 cannot be harmonized with the events surrounding the death of Antiochus IV. For this reason, some interpreters understand these verses to describe the Antichrist, who like Antiochus IV will persecute God’s people just before the second coming of Christ (cf. 12:1–3). These verses describe the character of the Antichrist, his activities, and the destiny of God’s people. This understanding requires a time interval between the events depicted in 11:21–35 and those in 11:36–12:3. Consequently, other interpreters have understood vv. 36–39 as a summary of Antiochus’s religious policies; vv. 40–45 as a description of how his ambition led to his defeat; and 12:1–3 as an anticipation of his defeat. The anticipated invasion of the Holy Land may be presented as a parallel to Nebuchadnezzar’s earlier invasion, using the names of the nations of that time, sparing Israel’s old enemies (v. 41), and climaxing in the anticipated defeat of Egypt itself (vv. 42, 43; cf. Ezek. 29). At his proudest moment, Antiochus was destroyed at Mount Zion in the heart of the Holy Land (vv. 44, 45). Antiochus’s defeat in 12:1–3 is described in terms of the absolute end of history. Because of the difficulties in interpreting 11:40–12:3, it is hard to discern how literal or metaphorical they are, and their interpretation must be speculative. The interpretation that the future Antichrist is in view will be followed in the remaining notes.

**11:36 till the indignation is accomplished.** Just as with Antiochus IV (8:17 note; 11:35), the time of persecution is subject to God’s control.

verse_quote: At the time of the end.
note: Here “end” carries an eschatological sense and refers to the end of this present age (8:17 note).
Palestine (cf. vv. 16, 45; 8:9).

See note on 10:13. God’s people will not be left alone in their hour of greatest need.

**a time of trouble.** This unparalleled time of trouble is sometimes identified with the “great tribulation” predicted by Jesus (Matt. 24:21; Mark 13:19).

**your people shall be delivered.** This deliverance is not necessarily from martyrdom (v. 2) but from the power of Satan, understood as his attempts to destroy people’s faith during the time of distress.

This verse is a clear prediction of the bodily resurrection of the godly and ungodly for the final judgment (Matt. 25:46; John 5:28, 29). This is what makes perseverance through times of great persecution worthwhile, even if it costs the faithful a painful martyrdom (see 11:33).
Sealing the book preserves it unaltered as it awaits fulfillment (8:26 note). The wise know where to find this wisdom, while the foolish run to and fro seeking answers in vain (see Amos 8:12).

verse_quote: How long ... what shall be the outcome.
note:
These are the key questions that are asked by those suffering under extreme persecution, and what follows answers these questions.

**a time, times, and half a time.** See note on 7:25. The period of persecution is limited in its scope by God.

**the shattering of the power of the holy people.** The progress of God’s work always proceeds through weakness, not strength.

In answer to the question in v. 8, the angel declares that the outcome of these things will be the perseverance of the saints through the refining fires of persecution, while the wicked display clearly their true colors. These attributes have already been seen in the experiences of Daniel and his friends.

verse_quote: the abomination that makes desolate is set up.
note:
See third note on 9:27. The similar activity of Antiochus IV prefigures this activity of the Antichrist (8:13).

**1,290 days.** The significance of these time frames is obscure. Three-and-a-half years is 1,260 days of a 360-day year, or 1,278 days of a 365-day year, and so if “a time, times and half a time” represents three-and-a-half years, the periods are roughly the same. The identification as three-and-a-half times focuses on the fact that this is a limited period of judgment rather than seven times (as in 4:16). Calling it 1,290 days reminds the reader that this is a precise period of time that God has planned down to the day.

Just when the faithful feel that the absolute limit of their endurance has been reached and they cannot endure any longer, they are asked to remain faithful for a few more days. The obscurity of this number underlines the fact that issues as to the timing of the end are a great mystery to all humans—even those with Daniel’s wisdom and insight (see v. 10)—but are under the control of God.
